content: A diabetes medication may protect against heart attacks and strokes through an unexpected biological mechanism. Two medications used in people with type 2 diabetes produced dramatically different results when scientists tested their ability to prevent dangerous blood clots. In mice with injured blood vessels, sotagliflozin reduced clot formation by approximately 60%, compared with just 5% to 10% for the widely prescribed drug empagliflozin. Researchers at Michigan Medicine also found that sotagliflozin suppresses excessive platelet activity, a process that can block blood flow to the heart or brain. Published in the Journal of Clinical Investigation , the findings suggest a possible explanation for the drug’s ability to reduce heart attack and stroke risk beyond its effects on blood sugar. Sotagliflozin, marketed as Inpefa, belongs to a group of medications called sodium-glucose cotransporter (SGLT) inhibitors. These drugs interfere with proteins that transport glucose through the body. Common treatments such as empagliflozin (Jardiance) and dapagliflozin (Farxiga) primarily block SGLT2, a protein that helps the kidneys reabsorb glucose. Sotagliflozin acts on both SGLT2 and SGLT1, which is also present in other tissues. Although SGLT2 inhibitors have established cardiovascular benefits, clinical trials have shown that sotagliflozin can also reduce ischemic events, including heart attacks and strokes. These occur when blood clots or other blockages restrict circulation. The researchers investigated whether the drug’s broader action on glucose transport proteins might help explain this protection. “A drug that can both decrease the risk for diabetes along with the risk for having a heart attack or stroke could be a turning point in our ability safely treat this growing population in the US and abroad,” said Michael A. Holinstat, Ph.D., M.S., co-senior author and professor of pharmacology, internal medicine, and surgery at the University of Michigan Medical School. Scientists compared sotagliflozin and empagliflozin using blood samples from healthy volunteers and people with type 2 diabetes. Sotagliflozin significantly reduced platelet activation and made platelets less likely to clump together. Empagliflozin produced little or no comparable effect. Platelets normally help stop bleeding by gathering at damaged blood vessels. However, excessive activation can produce clots inside arteries, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke. Sotagliflozin’s ability to suppress this activity may contribute to its cardiovascular benefits. “These experiments showed that sotagliflozin has a unique effect, and blocking SGLT2 alone is not enough to inhibit platelet aggregation,” said Eugene Chen, M.D., Ph.D., co-senior author and Frederick G. L. Huetwell Professor of Cardiovascular Medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School. “Sotagliflozin may offer additional protection against blood clots, potentially lowering the risk of heart attack and stroke.” The researchers next investigated whether inhibiting SGLT1 alone could account for sotagliflozin’s effects. When they genetically removed SGLT1 from mouse platelets, blood clot formation decreased by approximately 40%. However, neither this genetic approach nor treatment with mizagliflozin, a drug that selectively blocks SGLT1, fully reproduced sotagliflozin’s results. This suggests that other biological mechanisms contribute to the drug’s ability to prevent clot formation. One possibility involves SGLT1 in endothelial cells, which form the inner lining of blood vessels and interact with circulating platelets. Researchers have not yet established whether these cells contribute to sotagliflozin’s anti-clotting effects. “Sotagliflozin appears to be in the sweet spot because compounds that have higher levels of SGLT1-selective inhibitors can cause gastrointestinal issues,” said Bertram Pitt, M.D., co-author and professor emeritus of internal medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School. “We think this could be a wonder drug with potential to offer benefit for many conditions.” Sotagliflozin is FDA-approved to reduce certain cardiovascular risks in adults with heart failure and in adults with type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and additional cardiovascular risk factors. The researchers hope to investigate whether its effects on clotting could benefit patients with other conditions, including chronic kidney disease and atrial fibrillation, an irregular heart rhythm associated with increased stroke risk. The laboratory and animal findings provide evidence that sotagliflozin affects clotting through mechanisms beyond conventional SGLT2 inhibition. However, further clinical research is needed to determine how much this platelet effect contributes to preventing cardiovascular events in humans and whether it can do so without increasing bleeding complications. “The search for medications that reduce the risk of life-threatening blood clots without increasing the risk of bleeding has continued for decades,” Holinstat said. “Sotagliflozin has now been demonstrated to serve both functions and may represent the next advancement in prevention of blood clots, heart failure and stroke in patients with and without diabetes.” Reference: “SGLT1/2 inhibitor sotagliflozin, but not SGLT2-selective inhibitor empagliflozin, attenuates platelet activation and thrombosis” by Livia Stanger, Krista Goerger, Xu Zhang, Pooja Yalavarthi, Andrew Rickenberg, Adriana Yamaguchi, Mariane Flores Nascimento, Ashleigh Kilgore, Heeseo Kim, Xiaokang Wu, Yanhong Guo, Anna R. Dahlgren, Jifeng Zhang, Jordan A. Shavit, Bertram Pitt, Y. Eugene Chen and Michael Holinstat, 14 October 2026, The Journal of Clinical Investigation . A major clinical trial is challenging the effectiveness of commonly used injections for chronic Achilles tendon pain. A widely used injection treatment for chronic Achilles tendon pain may offer little lasting relief, according to a clinical trial published in The BMJ . Researchers found that high-volume injections, including those containing corticosteroids, did not significantly improve pain or physical function compared with a sham procedure after one year. The findings challenge the routine use of injections for a condition that can persist for years and interfere with everyday movement. Achilles tendinopathy causes pain, stiffness, and swelling in the tendon that connects the calf muscles to the heel. Approximately 6% of people experience the condition during their lifetime, and although exercise-based rehabilitation is the recommended treatment, up to 44% of patients do not recover. Many consequently explore other options, including injections intended to reduce pain and improve tendon function. To investigate whether these treatments provide meaningful benefits, researchers conducted a randomized clinical trial involving 192 adults with midportion Achilles tendinopathy in Melbourne, Australia, between December 2019 and July 2022. Participants were 49 years old on average, and their symptoms had persisted for a median of two years. The researchers divided participants into three groups receiving either a sham injection (64), a high-volume injection without corticosteroid (63), or a high-volume injection containing corticosteroid (65). The active injections delivered saline and local anesthetic around the affected tendon, with corticosteroid added in one group. Everyone also received the same exercise program, education, and guidance on modifying physical activity. The primary measure was pain and disability after 52 weeks, assessed using the Victoria Institute of Sport Assessment-Achilles scale (0-100, where 100 is no pain or disability). Participants began the trial with an average score of 48.7, indicating substantial symptoms and functional limitations. At the one-year follow-up, researchers obtained results from 181 participants (94%). Neither high-volume injection treatment produced a clear improvement in pain or disability compared with the sham procedure. The two active injection approaches also showed no meaningful difference in their overall outcomes. Injections without corticosteroid failed to outperform the placebo at any assessment point. Adding corticosteroid produced small improvements after six weeks, but these benefits were short-lived. By 26 weeks, participants who received corticosteroid had worse outcomes than those given high volume injections without the drug. An economic analysis found that corticosteroid-containing injections were less costly and generated more quality-adjusted life-years than sham treatment. However, the overall clinical results did not justify their routine use. No serious adverse events related to the trial treatments were reported. The researchers acknowledged several limitations. Many participants were recruited through social media, which could affect how well the findings apply to other patient populations. Clinicians administering the injections also knew which treatment they were providing, and some observed differences may have resulted from chance. Despite these uncertainties, the authors concluded that the evidence “should prompt clinicians to reconsider the rationale for using these injections in people with Achilles tendinopathy.” In a linked editorial, John Orchard of the University of Sydney cautioned that corticosteroids are neither universally beneficial nor inherently inappropriate. Their use should depend on the patient’s circumstances, particularly when immediate symptom relief takes priority over longer-term outcomes (where short-term needs predominate over longer-term needs). He emphasized that patients should never be told corticosteroid injections will fix or cure tendinopathy. “All clinicians recommending or performing corticosteroid injections for tendinopathy need to understand this trade-off and make every effort to explain the broader overview to the patient as part of the informed consent process,” he concluded. Reference: “Efficacy and cost effectiveness of high volume injections with and without corticosteroid compared with sham for midportion Achilles tendinopathy (Inject trial): randomised controlled trial” by Peter Malliaras, David Connell, Anders Ploug Boesen, Rebecca S Kearney, Hylton B Menz, Dylan Morrissey, Shannon E Munteanu, Karin Gravare Silbernagel, Martin Underwood, Andrew Forbes and Terry P Haines, 28 October 2026, BMJ .
